claims.text: A microstructure combining fine grains, high dislocation density, and a high density of nanoscale precipitates enhances hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
The primary load-bearing mechanisms are dislocation forest hardening and Orowan bypass of nanoscale precipitates.
Rapid solidification by selective laser melting can produce an equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA with elevated dislocation density.
The proposed rapidly solidified starting material has a fine cellular structure with nanoprecipitates at cell boundaries.
Precipitation behavior should be varied through thermal treatments or alloying additions while grain size and overall composition are kept similar.
Relevant mechanical testing spans room temperature through approximately 700 °C at an initial strain rate near 10^-3 s^-1.
Nanoscale oxide or intermetallic particles decorate grain or cell boundaries.
The rapidly solidified HEA contains an elevated intrinsic dislocation network.
High dislocation density raises strength through increased forest interactions among dislocations.
Nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion through the Orowan bypass mechanism.
Forest hardening and Orowan strengthening contribute synergistically to yield strength and hardness.
At comparable composition and grain size, a higher number density of smaller nanoscale precipitates will produce higher hardness and yield strength than fewer or coarser precipitates.
The proposed strengthening improvement should remain observable through approximately 700 °C.
Precipitate strengthening has an optimum precipitate size and number-density range.
A baseline containing fewer or coarser precipitates provides less obstruction to dislocation motion.
The proposed mechanism should dominate when grain size remains below approximately 10 µm.
Below approximately 700 °C, grain-boundary sliding and full recrystallization should not yet dominate the mechanical response.
At higher temperatures, thermal activation or precipitate coarsening may reduce the effectiveness of the proposed strengthening.
The quantitative strengthening depends on precipitate size and density, precipitate-matrix interface character, and local chemical fluctuations.
Failure to observe a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase in the higher-precipitate-density samples is specified as a falsifying result.
